newsitem.title: GERMANY: Nuclear train mishap horrifies German Greens.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear train mishap horrifies German Greens.

text.p: German ecology groups reacted with horror on Tuesday after a train carrying nuclear waste derailed in France, saying it proved what they had always said -- that nuclear shipments were potentially lethal and should be stopped.
The opposition Social Democrats and the Greens party urged Bonn to give a public explanation and take urgent measures to prevent more accidents.

French and German officials said it was not clear how the accident just over the German border in France happened, but gave assurances there had been no leakage of radioactivity. the train had been en route to a processing plant in Britain.
The German government defended its record saying that in the last 20 years some 1,500 nuclear waste shipments had left Germany to be processed in Britain or France without any serious incidents.

But the Greens party said the accident was one of a series of recent nuclear mishaps including an incident at Britain's Sellafield plant on Sunday in which six workers were contaminated by radioactive dust.

"These incidents are the logical consequence of a policy which consistently ignores the incalculable risks of atomic energy to both people and the environment, and focuses on economic interests," the party said in a statement."

Michael Mueller, SPD environment spokesman in parliament, told Berlin's Info Radio the accident proved how justified past warnings had been: "There are certain disaster scenarios for which containers have not been fully tested even today."
"These shipments must end. We must try to find a reasonable way of dealing with the problem. But shunting (nuclear waste) across Europe is thoroughly irresponsible," Mueller said.
Greenpeace warned Bonn that if the train had been involved in a high-speed collision with another train, it could have led to a "catastrophic leakage of radioactivity".

Germany's anti-nuclear activists have in recent years focused on stopping nuclear waste shipments -- a campaign that has involved sabotaging railway lines, bomb threats and massive sit-down demos on the rails.

The campaign reached a climax last year and was met with once of post-war Germany's biggest security operations. More than 19,000 police and border guards were called in to ensure a shipment reached Gorleben medium-term nuclear waste depot, near Hanover.

Bonn's Environment Ministry, however, countered that even in the event of a collision there would have been no leakage from the British-built Excellox 6 containers, carrying 18 spent fuel elements from the Lingen power station in eastern Germany.

"Large quantities of nuclear waste, such as spent nuclear rods, are transported in these containers, which are accident-proof," a ministry statement said. The 92-tonne metal containers undergo a series of tests under extreme conditions to prove virtual indestructibility before use, it said.

Tests include being dropped from a height of nine metres onto a steel plate, exposure to a temperature of 800 degrees celsius, being dropped 1.2 metres on a metal spike and being left 200 metres underwater for one hour, it said.
"Only certain types of container have been tested and those tests were not complete. According to my sources, there are still unanswered questions," said Mueller of the SPD.
"These tests do no reflect the real catastrophe scenario," Greenpeace quoted their nuclear expert Helmut Hirsch as saying.
"Such containers do not withstand collision at high speed or persistent fire at high temperatures. Radioactivity would still leak polluting the environment and damaging our health."
